Lesson 1 · Business route

Build evidence you can trust

Which lodging offer can we recommend with confidence?

The business problem

A travel coordinator must book a two-night stay for a visiting team. The request has several conditions: the arrival date is fixed, the room must be suitable, the walk must be reasonable, and the booking must be refundable. Finance asks for the lowest cost that meets those requirements. The export lists prices, but its rows describe offers on particular dates rather than interchangeable hotels. The coordinator needs a shortlist the booking team can use immediately.

What the data show

The booking file starts with 61 offer rows. After checking the key, defining the relevant market and removing incomplete records, 37 comparable offers remain.

The row count is part of the answer. A duplicate can make one offer appear twice; a missing charge can make an offer appear cheaper than it is. Once the eligible rows are identified, the coordinator calculates the same two-night total for each: room nights, cleaning, and tax. Sorting the nightly rate alone would answer a different question. The shortlist should show how the original export became a set of comparable offers, so a corrected quote can be traced to the ranking.

What would you decide?

Compare the full two-night cost for offers that meet the same requirements. Record every exclusion before ranking. A cheaper row is not automatically a better or even a valid offer.

Send the preferred offer and two backups with total cost, walking time, cancellation deadline, and the time each quote was checked. Keep excluded offers in a separate review list with the reason for exclusion. Before purchasing, verify the live price and terms. If the first option disappears, staff can apply the same eligibility and cost rule to the next one without asking the analyst to start again.

Pause and explain

If a join creates more rows than either source table, should the manager trust the resulting ranking?

Compare your reasoning

No. Check the join keys and row counts first. Duplicate matches can change prices, weights and rankings.

Check your judgment

Reveal the case’s known answer

The case includes one duplicate and three incomplete records in the selected market. The row-count trail explains how the shortlist was formed.

The bigger picture

A reliable recommendation begins before any calculation. The team has to agree what one row represents, which options meet the business requirements, and what total cost means. Those choices shape every later chart or model. The booking shortlist is one example of a general management habit: make the decision rule explicit, preserve the path from raw records to the options considered, and give the person taking action a result they can use. The next lesson asks what the full spread of those options tells us.
